state.case_summary:
A 64-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, chills, or fever. She had no history of hepatitis, surgery, or hereditary disease, and no underlying medical conditions. On examination, she was afebrile and oriented; there was right upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or palpable masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, and negative Murphy’s sign and shifting dullness.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• AFP 2.4 µg/l (normal 0.0–7.0)  
• CEA 11.6 µg/l (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• CA-125 32.3 KIU/l (normal 0.0–35.0)  
• CA19-9 228.0 KIU/l (normal 0.0–30.0)  
• Other liver enzymes and blood counts largely within reference ranges, except WBC 11.9×10^9/l (normal 3.5–9.5×10^9/l).

Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous echoic mass near the gallbladder fossa in the right liver lobe, calcifications in the right liver, multiple gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening, and enhanced pancreatic echogenicity. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a lesion in the right hepatic lobe adjacent to the gallbladder fossa, multiple enlarged hepatic hilar lymph nodes, and findings of gallstones with cholecystitis. Liver MRI demonstrated an occupying lesion in the right lobe with mild intrahepatic bile duct dilatation, raising the possibility of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, along with gallstones and cholecystitis. No extrahepatic primary tumor was identified.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Primary squamous cell carcinoma of the liver
B. Cholangiocarcinoma was considered because imaging “suggesting the possibility of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma” on MRI
C. Hepatocellular carcinoma was considered because HCC “usually shows marked arterial phase enhancement … with rapid
D. Hepatic cyst was considered because substantial necrosis in PSCCL “may resemble those of hepatic cysts,” although
E. Metastatic tumors were considered because metastatic liver lesions “usually present as single or multiple hypodense
F. Liver abscess was considered because on CT “a liver abscess appears as a round hypodense lesion with enhanced walls

root.label: Subacute Right Upper Abdominal Pain Syndrome with Elevated Tumor Markers and Hepatic Mass
supporting_facts: 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain
heterogeneous echoic mass near the gallbladder fossa in the right liver lobe on ultrasonography
multiple gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening
enlarged hepatic hilar lymph nodes on CT
excluded_candidates: Cholecystitis: while gallbladder wall thickening and gallstones are present, the presence of a hepatic mass and elevated tumor markers suggest a more complex diagnosis
Hepatitis: patient has no history of hepatitis and liver enzymes are largely within reference ranges
salient_findings: heterogeneous echoic mass in right liver lobe
